must_contain:
You've felt that your little one is real now, so talking to them afterward isn't just pretending.

## The Parent You Inherited

I'd look at the parent "script" you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it's often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like "You can come back to the table when you're done with your embarrassing crying fit." If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn't allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.

If it's a critic, the parent you inherited also measures whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, and then attacks you from both sides: you're not good enough, and anything that does look good is fake anyway. That second one means nothing you do could ever count, and it's one place feeling fake can come from. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying "Trust me," of course your little one doesn't answer.

But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don't have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.

must_contain_exact: ### When to Change the Strategy

Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I'd want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never had to find out. Before either one, I'd look for what exactly is in the way. Sometimes those weeks were mostly reading about it and getting ready, which can feel a lot like doing it (this article included). Or you did sit down with your little one, and fear got there first, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. It can be as plain as never having the place to yourself. Whatever it turns out to be, I'd work on that one thing instead of giving up on everything.

Maybe you've been trying to comfort your little one for weeks, and the words are all there, but the loving grown-up behind them isn't, not yet. Some people at that point might try saying sweeter and sweeter things, and then upon that not working, perhaps just "throw the baby out with the bathwater," and decide reparenting is useless. I'd borrow that grown-up first. Then try again, and see if your little one can tell the difference.

One more thing about telling whether it helped. A few hours of feeling lighter, with the old feeling back the same day, is a few hours of relief. I'd take that! I just wouldn't call the problem solved from it, or give the exercise all the credit, especially if you also slept well for once. Jot down what changed and how long it lasted if you want, and then leave it alone.

How many tries is enough? I really don't know, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who promises you a number, including you, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it's making things worse, or you just can't do it right now, I'd change course sooner (stopping counts). Not wanting to do it anymore is a reason too, but if that "nope" sounds like a part of you that's trying to protect you, I'd hear it out first. If it still says no, that's your answer. And if you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results, consider if you have a unique case these steps don't match yet. Maybe you'll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I'd do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I'd like to hear about it!

Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you're skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people's first guess is that they didn't go deep enough. I don't think that's it, though, and I don't think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn't come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I'd try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations. It doesn't have to happen after every session.

must_contain_exact: And if the grown-up you is there, and it's just how deep you're going that's too much, I'd go shallower. Like the flight attendants say, it's good to know where the exits are. 😅 So can you stop in the middle and come back to the room? If you can't, or going in at all keeps making it worse, I'd come all the way back out first. Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it. Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though. Now there's a grown-up around who can say, "Okay, that's enough for today," and try something gentler instead of giving up on them. Even just saying hi to them with your eyes open, before any imagery, counts.

A full break from your little one is a last resort. Sometimes it isn't up to you, though, like when something's actually unsafe. If you do need one, I'd jot down why, and how far you'd gotten before it got to be too much. A couple of lines on your phone is plenty. After a while away, it gets hard to remember. So once that reason has changed and you want to come back, the note tells you where it was still okay. I'd start there, or somewhere a bit gentler.

Whatever you try from that map, I wouldn't go just by how pleasant a session felt to tell whether it was too much. This kind of work can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes hard dreams, or stuff you'd rather never have met. And being present through all of it doesn't mean it wasn't too much. It's a bit like the gym, where sore and injured can feel pretty similar that evening, and it's the next few days that tell you which one it was.

So how were the next few days? How did you sleep, and could you get through your day okay? Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no? (And was it hard but doable, or just too much? A lot of the time you just know.) If you honestly can't tell yet, I wouldn't rush to call it healing or harm. I'd just make the next one a bit easier (shorter, or shallower, at a better time of day, with your eyes open, a teddy bear standing in for your little one, or a friend in the next room), one change at a time, so you learn what made the difference.

Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you're recovering well. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you're looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

If being alone was a big part of what hurt in the first place, then reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Do you have to get yourself sorted out first, so you'll be better company? I really don't think so. If the hurt was being alone, waiting just means more of being alone. So I'd call somebody or show up somewhere, mess and all.

I can't tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I'd bet on more than one place. Keep the good people you've already got. Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if one really fits you. Not every one of them has to click (nobody's taking attendance). And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that's where I'd want the Protector paying attention.

must_contain_exact: If picturing your little one feels fake, like you're just making it up, a real photo of you as a child can help, since there's no face or posture to invent. Yes, yes, it might feel a bit strange, seeing your own face from back then. But look at it gently and just notice what comes up.

While you look, notice what your body does and what feelings or urges show up. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you'll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then ("You hated that coat"). It might just be an inference you're guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up, which is also completely OK. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

We don't need to ask it leading questions, like "Who abused me & how?" or "What memory is my body hiding?" Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren't necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important. Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions, so we gotta be careful about that. Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it. I'm sure you can relate.
A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed... not necessarily representative. Flipping thru an album may give different jolts in your body.

If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don't confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here. You might be looking at the photo thinking, "That would explain so much." Journal what came up and how it came up, and see if you can get support from someone level-headed who won't lead you toward an answer.

must_contain: We all need some support, especially when taking our first steps. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide.

Inner Child Reparenting therapists do exist, and you can find them, although they often are not licensed, and I don't know of any central directory, nor of any protocol they'd have in common. There are none which work with my guide yet. I can consult, and if you like the guide, you can ask a therapist to check it out and see what they agree with or disagree with as a great way to vet them.

The best licensed, listed therapists you'll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I'll talk more about those in the appendix, but Schema Therapy comes closest to my approach. Open Path Collective (or a similar resource in your country) lists thousands of affordable therapists. You can filter them by Schema or IFS. You can often find even more Schema therapists at the official site.

Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I'd especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won't tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I'd also want one who doesn't put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won't charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can't tell you any of that.

Regarding AI therapy, I've tried all the top AI therapy apps, and they're all pretty bad. I'm trying to make my own based on this guide, but I'm becoming more convinced that unsupervised AI therapy is just a toss up. That doesn't mean you can't get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, though, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes.

Here's the idea behind Inner Child Reparenting, in a nutshell:

Growing up, all of us picked up automatic ways of understanding situations we find ourselves in, reacting based on those understandings, and then treating ourselves partly based on how we happened to handle things. Some of those patterns are wise in general, although even then, we are always learning from what life throws at us. Others of those patterns were built for a crisis that’s long over, and some just seem to make every situation worse.

Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding an Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding. At first, it’s deliberate, even awkward. With time, the roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing. You can always slow down and look closer when it helps.

must_contain_exact: ### Two Common Guarding Patterns Blocking Reparenting

One of these patterns is a skeptic, on duty all the time: "You're just making this up." It may have spent years keeping you from being humiliated or abandoned again, and it has probably watched you get excited about other healing things before that got unexplainedly dropped a month later. We do need some skepticism, so thank it for keeping you on track.

The other one shows up when you get close to some painful memory or insight. Suddenly you'd rather check your phone, or do anything aside from directly feeling it (even a yawn can come with an "I'm so done with this" feeling). Maybe this guard doesn't believe there's a grown-up around who could handle what's coming? That yawn might actually be the opposite of checking out, though. Re-evaluation Counseling, a global movement of peer counseling, counts yawning as productive emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out. The skeptic and the pull both started out guarding you against something that really hurt. If you treat either one like an enemy, it'll probably just think "See? I knew it," and it stays on the payroll since guards require attackers.

Say you learned somewhere along the way that if you need someone, they end up leaving you. You probably never said it to yourself in words, but it steers you before you know why. That pull of distraction is one way of dealing with it. Many folks will also find themselves going along with things they don't really prefer, or else insisting they don't need anybody (sour grapes). Some people pleasers go along for months as if nothing's wrong while the pressure builds and then they blow up out of nowhere. Then they feel so bad about it they go right back to going along to get along. With any of these patterns, I'd ask what it's protecting you from, because it doesn't really help to just label it a bad habit. (Sometimes a sweet is just a sweet, though, not an escape, as The Inner Guide gets into.)

You're actually a prophet, but you didn't know it! Have you ever heard of a self-fulfilling prophecy? Say nobody ever hears that you're struggling, since you didn't think they'd want to. Then nobody offers to help, and that can look like proof nobody cares. Keeping quiet might have been the smartest thing you could do back then, with nobody safe to tell, but now, if there are people who are safely available, it can keep help away.
In the process of self-differentiation, we learn to notice when we're making the trade, and we begin keeping our ground more when feasible.
